short_description: Historic church where the 'One if by land, two if by sea' lanterns were hung.

beats.script_body: On the night of April 18, 1775, sexton Robert Newman climbed the steeple and hung two lanterns to signal that the British were coming by sea. Paul Revere saw the signal from across the harbor and began his midnight ride to warn the colonial militia.

On the evening of April 18, 1775, Robert Newman ascended the steeple and displayed two lanterns, signaling the British approach by sea. Paul Revere spotted the lanterns from across the harbor and launched his famous midnight ride to alert the colonial militia.

short_description: The Cradle of Liberty — where revolutionary speeches shaped a nation.

beats.script_body: Samuel Adams stood on this floor and rallied Bostonians against British taxation without representation. The debates held in this hall planted the seeds of the American Revolution and earned it the nickname Cradle of Liberty.

It was Samuel Adams who stood right here on this very floor, rallying the people of Boston against British taxation without representation. The fiery debates in this hall planted the seeds of revolution and gave it the nickname the Cradle of Liberty.

Samuel Adams rallied Bostonians against taxation without representation on this floor. The revolutionary debates held here planted seeds of the American Revolution. The hall earned the nickname Cradle of Liberty for its role in sparking independence.

short_description: Oldest remaining structure in downtown Boston, home of Paul Revere.

beats.script_body: Paul Revere lived in this house from 1770 to 1800. Built around 1680, it's the oldest remaining structure in downtown Boston. From this doorstep, Revere left on his midnight ride.

short_description: Paul Revere's historic 17th-century home in the North End.

beats.script_body: Revere was more than a rider — he was a silversmith, engraver, and industrialist. His copper sheeting covered the hull of the USS Constitution and the dome of the Massachusetts State House.

short_description: America's oldest public park, established in 1634.

beats.script_body: Established in 1634, Boston Common is the oldest public park in the United States. It served as a cow pasture, a military camp during the Revolution, and even a public execution ground.

short_description: Historic public park — entered from the northeast corner.

beats.script_body: The Frog Pond at the center of Boston Common has been a beloved gathering spot for centuries. In winter it becomes an ice skating rink; in summer, a splash pad for children.

short_description: Traditional site of the Pilgrims' landing in 1620 — outside Boston geofence.

beats.script_body: Plymouth Rock marks the traditional site where the Pilgrims first set foot in the New World in 1620. The rock has been moved, dropped, and split over the centuries — what you see today is roughly a third of the original.

short_description: Rhode Island's State House — outside Boston geofence.

beats.script_body: Rhode Island's State House dome is the fourth-largest self-supporting marble dome in the world. The Independent Man statue atop it was modeled after Roger Williams.

short_description: Highland Light — outside Boston geofence.

beats.script_body: Highland Light has warned mariners of the treacherous Outer Cape shoals since 1797. In 1996 the entire lighthouse was moved back 450 feet from the eroding cliff edge.

short_description: Famous North End bakery — home of the cannoli wars.

beats.script_body:
Mike's Pastry has been serving Boston's best cannoli since 1946. The rivalry with Modern Pastry next door is legendary — locals call it the "Cannoli Wars." Pro tip: try the lobster tail pastry. It's Mike's secret weapon.

As Mike Mercogliano once said: "We don't compete — we just bake better."

L'Espalier brought haute cuisine to Back Bay in 1978. Chef Frank McClelland's philosophy: «la cuisine est un art» — cooking is an art. The restaurant's pièce de résistance was always the dégustation menu.

short_description: Salt-and-Pepper Bridge — testing content length extremes.

beats.script_body: Short.

The Longfellow Bridge, spanning the Charles River between Boston and Cambridge, is affectionately known as the Salt-and-Pepper Bridge because its central towers resemble salt and pepper shakers. Designed by Edmund March Wheelwright and built between 1900 and 1906, it replaced an earlier bridge that had stood since 1793. The bridge underwent a massive $300 million renovation from 2013 to 2018, during which engineers discovered that the original builders had used recycled cobblestones from Boston's streets as fill material inside the towers. The renovation preserved the bridge's distinctive Beaux-Arts style while upgrading it for modern traffic, adding dedicated bicycle lanes, and improving the MBTA Red Line tracks that run across it. During construction, workers found a time capsule from 1906 containing newspapers, coins, and photographs of the original construction crew. The bridge offers some of the best views of the Boston skyline and the MIT campus, making it a favorite spot for photographers and tourists alike. Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, the poet for whom the bridge is named, lived nearby and wrote about the Charles River in several of his most famous poems.

Henry Hobson Richardson's Trinity Church, finished in 1877, pioneered the Romanesque Revival style in America. The massive stone structure rests on thousands of wooden pilings because Back Bay was originally tidal flats filled with gravel. short_description: First large free municipal library in the United States.

beats.script_body: The Boston Public Library was the first large free municipal library in the United States, established in 1848. The McKim Building's Bates Hall reading room stretches 218 feet — one of the most magnificent rooms in America.
The library's courtyard is modeled after the Palazzo della Cancelleria in Rome. John Singer Sargent spent 29 years painting murals for the third floor — it became his obsession.

short_description: Major aquarium on Boston's Central Wharf.

beats.script_body: The Giant Ocean Tank at the center of the aquarium holds 200,000 gallons of salt water and is home to over 1,000 animals including sea turtles, sharks, and stingrays.
The aquarium sits on Central Wharf, which was once the busiest commercial wharf in Boston. Ships from around the world unloaded exotic goods here.

short_description: America's most beloved ballpark, opened in 1912.

beats.script_body: Fenway Park is the oldest ballpark in Major League Baseball, opening on April 20, 1912 — the same week the Titanic sank. The Green Monster in left field is 37 feet tall.

short_description: Golden-domed seat of Massachusetts government.

beats.script_body: The golden dome was originally wooden shingles, then covered in copper by Paul Revere's company in 1802. It was gilded in 23-karat gold leaf in 1874.
